fanoutqa_034459.t: Neil Armstrong :: Astronaut career :: Gemini program :: Gemini 5 :: chunk_0010
fanoutqa_034459.x:
Neil Armstrong :: Astronaut career :: Gemini program :: Gemini 5 :: chunk_0010
On February 8, 1965, Armstrong and Elliot See were picked as the backup crew for [Gemini 5](/wiki/Gemini_5 "Gemini 5"), with Armstrong as commander, supporting the prime crew of [Gordon Cooper](/wiki/Gordon_Cooper "Gordon Cooper") and [Pete Conrad](/wiki/Pete_Conrad "Pete Conrad").[[74]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReichl201678-74) The mission's purpose was to practice [space rendezvous](/wiki/Space_rendezvous "Space rendezvous") and to develop procedures and equipment for a seven-day flight, all of which would be required for a mission to the Moon. With two other flights ([Gemini 3](/wiki/Gemini_3 "Gemini 3") and [Gemini 4](/wiki/Gemini_4 "Gemini 4")) in preparation, six crews were competing for simulator time, so Gemini 5 was postponed. It finally lifted off on August 21.[[75]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHackerGrimwood2010255–256-75) Armstrong and See watched the launch at [Cape Kennedy](/wiki/Cape_Kennedy "Cape Kennedy"), then flew to the [Manned Spacecraft Center](/wiki/Manned_Spacecraft_Center "Manned Spacecraft Center") (MSC) in Houston.[[76]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHansen2005239-76) The mission was generally successful, despite a problem with the [fuel cells](/wiki/Fuel_cell "Fuel cell") that prevented a rendezvous. Cooper and Conrad practiced a "phantom rendezvous", carrying out the maneuver without a target.[[77]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHackerGrimwood2010257–258-77)

Main article: [Economy of Japan](/wiki/Economy_of_Japan "Economy of Japan")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/71/Nakanoshima_Skyscrapers_in_201504_001.jpg/250px-Nakanoshima_Skyscrapers_in_201504_001.jpg)](/wiki/File:Nakanoshima_Skyscrapers_in_201504_001.jpg)

Skyscrapers in [Nakanoshima](/wiki/Nakanoshima "Nakanoshima"), Osaka; a major [financial center](/wiki/Financial_center "Financial center") in Japan

Japan has the world's [fourth-largest economy by nominal GDP](/wiki/List_of_countries_by_GDP_(nominal) "List of countries by GDP (nominal)"), after that of the United States, China and Germany; and the [fifth-largest by PPP-adjusted GDP](/wiki/List_of_countries_by_GDP_(PPP) "List of countries by GDP (PPP)").[[172]](#cite_note-173) As of 2023, [Japan's labor force](/wiki/Labor_market_of_Japan "Labor market of Japan") is the world's [tenth-largest](/wiki/List_of_countries_by_labour_force "List of countries by labour force"), consisting of over 69.2 million workers.[[85]](#cite_note-cia-86) As of 2024, Japan has a [low unemployment rate](/wiki/List_of_countries_by_unemployment_rate "List of countries by unemployment rate") of around 2.6%.[[173]](#cite_note-174) [Its poverty rate](/wiki/Poverty_in_Japan "Poverty in Japan") is the second highest among the G7 countries,[[174]](#cite_note-175) and exceeds 15.7% of the population.[[175]](#cite_note-176) Japan has the highest ratio of public debt to GDP among advanced economies,[[176]](#cite_note-177) with [a national debt](/wiki/National_debt_of_Japan "National debt of Japan") estimated at 237% relative to GDP as of 2026.[[177]](#cite_note-178) The [Japanese yen](/wiki/Japanese_yen "Japanese yen") is the world's third-largest [reserve currency](/wiki/Reserve_currency "Reserve currency") after the US dollar and the euro.[[178]](#cite_note-179)

In 2024, Japan was the world's [eight-largest exporter](/wiki/List_of_countries_by_exports "List of countries by exports")[[179]]

As of 2026, this list includes all 98 buildings (completed and architecturally [topped out](/wiki/Topping_out "Topping out")) that reach a height of 350 m (1,150 ft) or more, as assessed by their highest architectural feature. The building is considered as architecturally topped out when it is under construction, structurally topped out, fully clad, and the highest finished architectural elements are in place.[[10]](#cite_note-:1-10)

Of these buildings, almost half are in China. Six of the last seven buildings to have held the record as "[tallest building](/wiki/Skyscraper#History_of_the_tallest_skyscrapers "Skyscraper")" are still found in the list, with the exception being [the North Tower](/wiki/1_World_Trade_Center_(1970%E2%80%932001) "1 World Trade Center (1970–2001)") of the original [New York](/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") [World Trade Center](/wiki/World_Trade_Center_(1973%E2%80%932001) "World Trade Center (1973–2001)") at 417 m (1,368 ft) after its destruction in the [September 11 attacks](/wiki/September_11_attacks "September 11 attacks") of 2001. Had the World Trade Center Twin Towers never been destroyed and [One World Trade Center](/wiki/One_World_Trade_Center "One World Trade Center") never built, they would have ranked 39 and 40 on the list today.

fanoutqa_024987.t: French Bulldog :: History :: Breed clubs and modern recognition :: chunk_0002
fanoutqa_024987.x:
French Bulldog :: History :: Breed clubs and modern recognition :: chunk_0002
Americans had been importing French Bulldogs for a while, but it was not until 1885 that they were brought over in order to set up an American-based breeding program. They were mostly owned by society ladies, who first displayed them at the [Westminster Kennel Club Dog Show](/wiki/Westminster_Kennel_Club_Dog_Show "Westminster Kennel Club Dog Show") in 1896.[[9]](#cite_note-snr-9) In the following year, the judge at the dog show, George Raper, only chose winners with "rose ears"—ears that folded at the tip, as with the standard for Bulldogs.[[10]](#cite_note-10) The ladies formed the French Bull Dog Club of America and created a [breed standard](/wiki/Breed_standard_(dogs) "Breed standard (dogs)") which preferred the "erect bat ear" type.[[5]](#cite_note-coile-5): 7In the early 20th century, the breed remained in vogue for high society, with dogs changing hands for up to $3,000 and being owned by members of influential families such as the [Rockefellers](/wiki/Rockefeller_family "Rockefeller family") and the [J. P. Morgans](/wiki/J._P._Morgan "J. P. Morgan"). The [American Kennel Club](/wiki/American_Kennel_Club "American Kennel Club") recognized the breed quickly after the breed club was formed, and by 1906 the French Bulldog was the fifth most popular dog breed in America.[[5]](#cite_note-coile-5): 8

This new Bulldog breed arrived for the first time in England in 1893, with English Bulldog breeders in an uproar as the French imports did not meet the new breed standards in place by this time, and they wanted to prevent the English stock from crossbreeding with the French. [The Kennel Club](/wiki/The_Kennel_Club "The Kennel Club") initially recognized them as a subset of the existing Bulldog breed rather than an entirely new breed.[[5]](#cite_note-coile-5): 6 Some English breeders in this period bred the French Bulldogs in order to resurrect the Toy Bulldog.[[6]](#cite_note-leighton-6): 58

Main article: [Sport in South America](/wiki/Sport_in_South_America "Sport in South America")

A wide range of sports are played in the continent of South America, with [football](/wiki/Association_football "Association football") being the most popular overall, while baseball is the most popular in Venezuela.

Other sports include basketball, [cycling](/wiki/Cycle_sport "Cycle sport"), [polo](/wiki/Polo "Polo"), volleyball, [futsal](/wiki/Futsal "Futsal"), [motorsports](/wiki/Motorsports "Motorsports"), [rugby](/wiki/Rugby_football "Rugby football") (mostly in Argentina and Uruguay), [handball](/wiki/Handball "Handball"), tennis, golf, [field hockey](/wiki/Field_hockey "Field hockey"), [boxing](/wiki/Boxing "Boxing"), and [cricket](/wiki/Cricket "Cricket").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/58/Maracan%C3%A3_2014_f.jpg/250px-Maracan%C3%A3_2014_f.jpg)](/wiki/File:Maracan%C3%A3_2014_f.jpg)

[Maracanã Stadium](/wiki/Maracan%C3%A3_Stadium "Maracanã Stadium") in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

South America hosted its first [Olympic Games](/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games") in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in 2016, and has hosted the [Youth Olympic Games](/wiki/Youth_Olympic_Games "Youth Olympic Games") in Buenos Aires, Argentina, in 2018. **Mercury** is the first [planet](/wiki/Planet "Planet") from the [Sun](/wiki/Sun "Sun") and the [smallest in the Solar System](/wiki/List_of_Solar_System_objects_by_size "List of Solar System objects by size"). It is a [rocky planet](/wiki/Rocky_planet "Rocky planet") with a [trace atmosphere](/wiki/Atmosphere_of_Mercury "Atmosphere of Mercury") and a surface [gravity](/wiki/Gravity "Gravity") slightly higher than that of [Mars](/wiki/Mars "Mars"). The surface of Mercury is similar to Earth's [Moon](/wiki/Moon "Moon"), being [cratered](/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater"), with an expansive [rupes](/wiki/Rupes "Rupes") system generated from [thrust faults](/wiki/Thrust_fault "Thrust fault"), and bright [ray systems](/wiki/Ray_system "Ray system"), formed by [ejecta](/wiki/Ejecta "Ejecta"). Its largest crater, [Caloris Planitia](/wiki/Caloris_Planitia "Caloris Planitia"), has a diameter of 1,550 km (960 mi), which is about one-third the diameter of the planet (4,880 km or 3,030 mi). Being the most [inferior](/wiki/Inferior_planet "Inferior planet") orbiting planet, it always appears close to the Sun in [Earth](/wiki/Earth "Earth")'s sky, either as a "morning star" or an "evening star". It is the planet with the highest [delta-v](/wiki/Delta-v "Delta-v") required for travel from Earth, as well as to and from the [other planets](/wiki/List_of_planets_in_the_Solar_System "List of planets in the Solar System") in the [Solar System](/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System").

Mercury's [sidereal year](/wiki/Sidereal_year "Sidereal year") (88.0 Earth days) and [sidereal day](/wiki/Sidereal_day "Sidereal day") (58.65 Earth days) are in a 3:2 ratio, in a [spin–orbit resonance](/wiki/Tidal_locking#Planets "Tidal locking"). Consequently, one solar day (sunrise to sunrise) on Mercury lasts for around 176 Earth days: twice the planet's sidereal year. Rankings have also been produced in the past by *[The Daily Telegraph](/wiki/The_Daily_Telegraph "The Daily Telegraph")* and the *[Financial Times](/wiki/Financial_Times "Financial Times")*.

British universities rank highly in [global university rankings](/wiki/College_and_university_rankings "College and university rankings") with eight featuring in the top 100 of all three major global rankings as of 2024: *[QS](/wiki/QS_World_University_Rankings "QS World University Rankings")*, *[Times Higher Education](/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings "Times Higher Education World University Rankings")*, and *[ARWU](/wiki/Academic_Ranking_of_World_Universities "Academic Ranking of World Universities")*. The national rankings differ from global rankings with a focus on the quality of [undergraduate education](/wiki/Undergraduate_education "Undergraduate education"), as opposed to [research](/wiki/Research "Research") prominence and faculty [citations](/wiki/Citation "Citation").

The primary aim of domestic rankings is to inform prospective undergraduate applicants about universities based on a range of criteria, including: entry standards, student satisfaction, staff–student ratio, expenditure per student, research quality, [degree classifications](/wiki/British_undergraduate_degree_classification "British undergraduate degree classification"), completion rates, and graduate outcomes. All of the league tables also rank universities in individual subjects.

QS World University Rankings :: Rankings :: QS World University Rankings :: Internationalization :: chunk_0005
The final 10% of a university's score is derived from measures intended to capture their internationalization: half from their percentage of international students, and the other half from their percentage of international staff. This is of interest partly because it shows whether a university is putting effort into global collaboration and diversity, but also because it indicates global appeal for students and researchers around the world.[[26]](#cite_note-26)

QS recently began distinguishing between International Faculty Ratio and International Student Ratio', both of which account for 5% of the total weightage. While the former evaluates the ratio of international faculty staff to overall staff, the latter assumes that Institutions that have a large number of international students should have better networking, cultural exchanges, a more diverse learning experience and alumni diversity.[[19]](#cite_note-britannia-study-19)
